# Introduction

In this post, I document the steps I took to set up a robotic system consisting of an SO-101 follower/leader arm pair, a Logitech Brio webcam, and a Raspberry Pi 5.

My long-term goal is to build a system that can play chess well enough to compete against a human.
The system would make use of ROS2 to split the different components into nodes (e.g. robot arm node, camera node, inference node, visualization node)
that communicate between each other through message passing using topics.
This post covers the first milestone: establishing a reliable data collection and policy deployment pipeline using a simpler ball-in-cup task. 

While experimenting with the [LeRobot](https://huggingface.co/docs/lerobot/index) library, I encountered a few bugs and submitted two PRs to fix them ([#3571](https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/pull/3571), [#3593](https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/pull/3593)), which I hope will be merged soon enough. 

This post serves mostly as a form of personal note taking, but I decided to share it in case it proves useful to someone else.

# Hardware

The hardware I used for the system is:

- **SO-101 motor kit**: I bought the kit without 3D printed parts from [SeeedStudio](https://www.seeedstudio.com/SO-ARM101-Low-Cost-AI-Arm-Kit-p-6426.html)
- **SO-101 3D printed parts**: I printed my own parts because I have a 3D printer and wanted to choose colors freely.
- **Raspberry Pi 5**: I had one that a friend gifted me for my birthday (Thanks, Oussama!)
- **Logitech Brio webcam**: My daily driver, repurposed for robot vision.

# Raspberry Pi Setup

## OS and Dependencies

For this project, I decided to use Ubuntu 24.04 on the Pi 5 instead of the more typical choice of Raspberry Pi OS,
because it has first-class support of ROS2 which I'm planning to use in a later phase.

Here's what I did:

- Flashed Ubuntu 24.04 via the [Raspberry Pi Imager](https://www.raspberrypi.com/software/).
- Plugged in keyboard, mouse, and screen for the initial setup. Unplugged them once SSH access was set up.
- Installed [FFmpeg](https://ffmpeg.org/) for video encoding.

## Remote Connectivity & SSH Configuration

Since the Pi will operate without a monitor, I set up secure SSH access immediately:

- Generated an SSH keypair on my workstation.
- Copied the public key using `ssh-copy-id pi@<ip>`
- Disabled password authentication in `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`
- Installed and configured mDNS by following instructions from [this post](https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-01-15-configure-mdns-avahi-ubuntu/view) so I can connect via `ssh pi@rpi-robotarm.local`
- Added an entry in my workstation's ssh configuration file (`~/.ssh/config`) with X11 forwarding for easier GUI debugging and SSH access.

  ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
  ### ~/.ssh/config

    ```default
    Host rpi-robotarm
        Hostname rpi-robotarm.local
        User pi
        PreferredAuthentications publickey
        IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_rpi
        ForwardX11 yes
    ```
  :::

## Changing Camera Zoom and Field-of-View

I needed a wider view to capture the full workspace. Unfortunately, Logitech's official configuration tools are Windows-only.

Fortunately, the open-source [Camera Controls](https://github.com/soyersoyer/cameractrls) tool fills the gap on Linux.

I set the zoom to 100% and adjusted the FoV to 90° for a clean, wide shot of the workspace.

# SO-101

The SO-101 is an open-source, affordable robot arm. I followed the official LeRobot [SO-101 tutorial](https://huggingface.co/docs/lerobot/so101) for assembly and motor initialization. The documentation is thorough if a bit confusing at times.

::: {.callout-note}
**3D Printing Note**: The SO-101's STL files require extensive support structures. If you're printing these yourself, consider printing in different orientations and changing some of the print parameters (e.g. layer height, support type) to improve print quality.
:::

## Setup and calibration

- Create virtual environment and install dependencies:

  ```bash
  python -m venv .venv
  source .venv/bin/activate
  pip install "lerobot[feetech,dataset,hardware]==0.5.1"
  ```

- Make sure everything works by running:

  ```bash
  lerobot-info
  ```

All commands below assume you're in the virtual environment created above.

### Setting motor IDs

```bash
lerobot-setup-motors --robot.type=so101_follower --robot.port=/dev/ttyACM0
```

```bash
lerobot-setup-motors --teleop.type=so101_leader --teleop.port=/dev/ttyACM1
```

### Calibrating the motors

```bash
lerobot-calibrate --robot.type=so101_follower --robot.port=/dev/ttyACM0 --robot.id=follower_arm
```

```bash
lerobot-calibrate --teleop.type=so101_leader --teleop.port=/dev/ttyACM1 --teleop.id=leader_arm
```

Each of these commands will ask you to first move the joints to the middle of their range and then to move them through their entire range of movement.

Once done, the calibration profiles will be saved under `~/.cache/huggingface/lerobot/calibration/robots/so_follower/follower_arm.json` and `~/.cache/huggingface/lerobot/calibration/teleoperators/so_leader/leader_arm.json`

### Teleoperation

Once the calibration is done and to test that everything works as expected, we try teleoperation by running:

```bash
lerobot-teleoperate \
    --robot.type=so101_follower \
    --robot.port=/dev/ttyACM0 \
    --robot.id=follower_arm \
    --teleop.type=so101_leader \
    --teleop.port=/dev/ttyACM1 \
    --teleop.id=leader_arm
```

The leader arm (with the handle) should now control the follower arm (with the gripper) in real-time.

# Imitation Learning

Imitation learning is a reinforcement learning approach where an agent learns to perform a task by supervised learning from expert demonstrations[^1]

[^1]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imitation_learning

I chose to use ACT (Action Chunking with Transformers) for this task because it's fast, lightweight, and surprisingly effective for fine manipulation and is also the recomended method by the LeRobot documentation for manipulation tasks[^2].

[^2]: https://huggingface.co/docs/lerobot/act

It was introduced in "Learning fine-grained bimanual manipulation with low-cost hardware"[^3]

[^2]: Zhao, Tony Z., et al. ["Learning fine-grained bimanual manipulation with low-cost hardware."](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.13705) arXiv preprint arXiv:2304.13705 (2023).

## Task

The task we'll be using consists of having the follower arm grab a ball and put it inside a cup (see @fig-ball-cup-setup).

The leader arm will be used to teleoperate the follower arm during data collections to do the task.

![Picture of the task setup](so101_ball_cup_setup.jpg){#fig-ball-cup-setup width=80%}

## Data Collection

Before training a model, we need expert demonstrations. LeRobot recommends around 50 episodes for a baseline policy.

::: {.callout-tip}
Vary the ball and cup positions across episodes. Diverse scenarios lead to a more robust policy.
:::


```sh
lerobot-record \
    --robot.type=so101_follower \
    --robot.port=/dev/ttyACM0 \
    --robot.id=follower_arm \
    --robot.cameras="{ front: {type: opencv, index_or_path: 0, width: 640, height: 480, fps: 30, warmup_s: 2}}" \
    --teleop.type=so101_leader \
    --teleop.port=/dev/ttyACM1 \
    --teleop.id=leader_arm \
    --dataset.repo_id=ball-cup \
    --dataset.num_episodes=50 \
    --dataset.episode_time_s=30 \
    --dataset.reset_time_s=10 \
    --dataset.single_task="Put ball in cup" \
    --dataset.streaming_encoding=true \
    --dataset.encoder_threads=2 \
    --dataset.push_to_hub=False
```

::: {#fig-ball-cup-demonstrations}

{{< video
    so101_ball_cup_demonstrations.mp4
    title="Example demonstrations for data collection"
    aria-label="Video showing 6 demonstrations of teleoperating the robot arm for data collection"
>}}

:::

## Training

Once the data collection was done, I copied the dataset over from the Raspberry PI to my desktop to train a model using my workstations's GPU.

```bash
lerobot-train \
    --dataset.repo_id=ball-cup_20260512_093538 \
    --output_dir=outputs/train/act_so101_ball_cup \
    --job_name=act_so101_ball_cup \
    --policy.push_to_hub=False \
    --policy.type=act \
    --policy.repo_id=ball_cup_policy \
    --policy.device=cuda
```



## Inference

Once the model training was done, I copied over the last checkpoint of the training and used to 

```bash
lerobot-rollout \
    --strategy.type=base \
    --policy.path=/home/pi/projects/lerobot/output/train/act_so101_ball_cup/checkpoints/last/pretrained_model/ \
    --robot.type=so101_follower \
    --robot.port=/dev/ttyACM0 \
    --robot.id=follower_arm \
    --robot.cameras="{ front: {type: opencv, index_or_path: 0, width: 640, height: 480, fps: 30, warmup_s: 2}}" \
    --task="Put ball in cup" \
    --duration=30
```

::: {#fig-ball-cup-policy}

{{< video
    so101_ball_cup_policy.mp4
    title="Demonstration of trained policy"
    aria-label="Video showing SO-101 robot arm controlled by the trained policy"
>}}

:::

The policy works, but it's not fully robust. Some rollouts succeed gracefully, while others fail due to release timing or trajectory hesitation. This is expected for a baseline ACT policy. In a follow-up post, I'll experiment with data augmentation and hyperparameter tuning.

# Conclusion

This was first phase of the project. I assembled everything and made sure the system works. I went through all the steps (data collection, training, rollout or inference).

In follow-up posts, will try to follow this rough roadmap:

- **Policy refinement**: I'll add data augmentation (randomized lighting, perspective shifts, jittered start positions) and run a hyperparameter sweep on the ACT chunk size and lookahead window with the aim of increasing the policy's success rate and robustness.
- **Chess perception**: Use the camera to detect the board state and classify piece positions. I will most likely start with a simple approach based on heuristics and if that doesn't work at all or not well enough then I would move towards fine-tuning a lightweight YOLO model.
- **Chess planning**: Use a chess engine, most likely [stockfish](https://stockfishchess.org/), to plan the next move and detect any illegal moves made by the human player.
- **Chess movement**: Train a policy to move the chess pieces based on the planning.
- **Modular architecture**: Decouple perception, planning, and control into independent ROS2 nodes that communicate through message passing.
- **Closed-loop play**: Test against a human. Track win/draw/loss ratios, log failure states, and iterate on the different layers.
